verse.text: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the assembly of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ:
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'church', which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew this word as the ordinary term for a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament's word for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution, so 'assembly' is used throughout this translation.

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'God our Father' here, matching verse 1 and Paul's usual greeting. The edition translated omits 'our', judging that scribes more likely added it to match the familiar formula than removed it. The evidence is closely divided.

verse.text: We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers and sisters, as is fitting, because your faith is growing abundantly and the love that every one of you has for one another is increasing,
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women. Since the letter is addressed to the whole assembly, 'brothers and sisters' gives what the first hearers understood. Many recent translations do the same.

verse.text: so that we ourselves boast about you in the assemblies of God, about your endurance and faith in all your persecutions and the afflictions you are bearing.
verse.note: The Greek word covers both 'faith' (trust) and 'faithfulness' (loyalty, reliability). Paired with endurance under persecution, it could well mean 'faithfulness' here, and some interpreters take it so. 'Faith' is kept because verse 3 has just used the same word for the Thessalonians' growing trust.

verse.text: This is evidence of God's just judgment, so that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are in fact suffering,
verse.note: In Greek this phrase is loosely attached to what precedes, and a new sentence has been started in English for clarity. It is not certain what the 'evidence' is. Most take it to be the Thessalonians' endurance and faith under persecution, while others take it to be the sufferings themselves, seen as part of God's process of fitting them for the kingdom.

Most translations have 'righteous judgment' here and then 'just' in verse 6, though the Greek word is the same. Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). Because the point in both verses is that God judges fairly, 'just' is used in both so the repetition is visible.

verse.text: since indeed it is just in God's sight to repay with affliction those who afflict you
and to give you who are afflicted relief along with us, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power
verse.note: The Greek reads literally 'angels of his power'. Most translations treat this as a Semitic idiom meaning 'his powerful angels'. It can also mean the angels who belong to and carry out his power, and the literal wording is kept here because it allows both senses.

verse.text: in flaming fire, bringing retribution on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the good news of our Lord Jesus.
verse.note: The traditional 'vengeance' can suggest personal vindictiveness. The Greek word belongs to the language of justice, meaning the carrying out of a deserved sentence or the vindication of the wronged. The phrase, together with 'in flaming fire', echoes the Greek text of Isaiah 66:15, where the Lord comes in fire to repay his enemies.

'Gospel' is the traditional rendering and remains common. The Greek word was an everyday term for good news or a welcome announcement, used for example of a victory or a ruler's accession. 'Good news' gives a modern reader what the original hearers heard.

verse.text: They will pay the penalty of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might,

note.term: away from the presence of the Lord
note.traditional: from the presence of the Lord

verse.note: The Greek preposition is simply 'from'. It may mean separation ('away from the Lord's presence'), as most modern translations take it, or source ('destruction that comes from the Lord's presence'). The wording echoes the Greek text of Isaiah 2:10, 19 and 21, where people hide from the face of the Lord and the glory of his might, which favours separation. The nature of 'eternal destruction', whether unending ruin or final annihilation, is debated and the Greek does not settle it.

verse.text: when he comes on that day to be glorified in his holy ones and to be marveled at in all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'saints', which now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. A few interpreters think angels are meant here, but the parallel with 'all who have believed' points to believers.

verse.text: To this end we also pray for you always, that our God may count you worthy of the calling and by his power bring to completion every desire for goodness and every work of faith,

note.traditional: all the good pleasure of his goodness / every resolve for good

verse.note: The Greek does not say whose 'good pleasure' or 'desire' this is. Older translations took it as God's own good pleasure, while most modern ones take it as the believers' desire to do good. The parallel with 'work of faith', which is clearly theirs, supports the modern reading. The verb rendered 'count you worthy' is likewise taken by some as 'make you worthy', though its ordinary meaning is 'deem worthy'.

verse.text: so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.

note.term: our God and the Lord Jesus Christ
note.traditional: our God and the Lord Jesus Christ

verse.note: In Greek a single article governs both 'God' and 'Lord', so the phrase can be read as 'our God and Lord, Jesus Christ', calling Jesus God. Most scholars prefer two persons, because 'Lord Jesus Christ' is a fixed expression that often stands without an article, as in verses 1 and 2. The grammar allows either reading.

verse.text: Now we ask you, brothers and sisters, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered to him,
verse.note: The Greek word means both arrival and presence, and was the regular term for the state visit of a king or emperor to a city. The same word is used in verse 9 for the arrival of the lawless one, which is presented as a counterfeit of the Lord's own coming.

verse.text: not to be quickly shaken from your good sense or alarmed, whether by a spirit or by a spoken word or by a letter supposedly from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come.
verse.note: This most likely means a prophetic utterance claimed to come from the Spirit, and some translations render it ‘by a prophecy’. It is also unclear whether ‘supposedly from us’ applies only to the letter or to all three channels.

Older English versions have ‘is at hand’, meaning near. The Greek perfect tense of this verb normally means ‘is present’ or ‘has arrived’, and most modern translations and commentators take it that way. The claim being corrected was that the day of the Lord was already here, not merely close.

verse.text: Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,
verse.note: These words are not in the Greek. The sentence begins with ‘unless’ and is never grammatically completed, so translations supply the missing main clause from verse 2. Nearly all agree on what must be supplied.

In the period the word meant revolt or defection, political or religious; in the Greek Old Testament it is used of rebellion against God. ‘Falling away’ suggests a gradual drift, which is weaker than the Greek. Whether a religious defection or a wider revolt against God is in view is debated; a few interpreters have proposed ‘departure’ in a spatial sense, but this has little lexical support.

Many later manuscripts read ‘man of sin’, which is the basis of the older English rendering. The earliest witnesses read ‘lawlessness’, which also fits ‘the mystery of lawlessness’ and ‘the lawless one’ in verses 7 and 8, and most modern editions adopt it.

‘Son of’ is a Semitic idiom for someone who belongs to or is marked out for something, so the phrase means one destined for destruction. ‘Perdition’ is no longer ordinary English. The word is related to the verb behind ‘those who are perishing’ in verse 10.

verse.text: who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.

note.term: takes his seat in the temple of God
note.traditional: sitteth in the temple of God

verse.note: The language echoes Daniel 11:36, where a king exalts himself above every god, a passage linked to the desecration of the Jerusalem temple by Antiochus IV. Readers would also have remembered the emperor Gaius (Caligula) ordering his statue set up in the temple around AD 40. Whether the Jerusalem temple, a heavenly temple, or the church is meant here is disputed.

verse.text: Do you not remember that I used to tell you these things while I was still with you?
And now you know what is restraining him, so that he may be revealed in his own time.

note.traditional: what withholdeth; what is restraining him

verse.note: The Greek has no object (‘him’ is supplied), and the restrainer is a thing in this verse and a person in verse 7. The readers had been told what was meant; later interpreters have not, and proposals include the Roman empire and emperor, God or the Spirit, the preaching of the gospel, and an angel. No view commands a consensus. ‘Now’ may also be read with the restraining: ‘you know what is now restraining him’.

verse.text: For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only the one who now restrains will do so until he is out of the way.
verse.note: In Jewish and early Christian usage the word means a secret, something hidden for the present and disclosed in due course, not a puzzle. Here it stands in contrast to ‘revealed’ in verses 6 and 8: lawlessness is already operating out of sight before it appears openly.

verse.text: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the manifestation of his coming.
verse.note: The Greek word means breath, wind or spirit; here it is breath. The phrase draws on Isaiah 11:4, where the coming king from David's line kills the wicked with the breath of his lips. The point is that no struggle is needed.

verse.text: The coming of the lawless one is by the working of Satan, with every kind of power and with lying signs and wonders,
and with every wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they did not welcome the love of the truth so as to be saved.
And for this reason God sends a delusion to work on them, so that they believe the lie,
so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in wickedness.

But we ought always to thank God for you, brothers and sisters loved by the Lord, because God chose you as firstfruits for salvation through being made holy by the Spirit and through faith in the truth.
verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between two readings that differ by a single letter: ‘as firstfruits’ and ‘from the beginning’. The SBL text reads ‘firstfruits’, the first portion of a harvest offered to God; many translations follow the other reading. Both are well attested and the choice is uncertain.

verse.text: To this he called you through our good news, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word meant an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler's accession; it was not yet a religious technical term or the name of a kind of book. ‘Gospel’ is the traditional rendering and means the same thing by origin, but many modern translations now use ‘good news’.

verse.text: So then, brothers and sisters, stand firm and hold on to the traditions you were taught, whether by our spoken word or by our letter.
Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and by grace gave us eternal encouragement and good hope,
encourage your hearts and strengthen them in every good deed and word.
Finally, brothers and sisters, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may race ahead and be glorified, just as it was among you,
verse.note: The Greek plural, used to address a whole congregation, included the women in it, and a first-century hearer would have understood it that way. Several recent translations render it this way. In verses 6 and 15 the generic singular is rendered "brother or sister" for the same reason.

verse.text: and that we may be rescued from perverse and evil people; for not everyone has faith.
But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.
verse.note: The Greek form can be masculine ("the evil one", meaning Satan) or neuter ("evil" in general). Most modern translations choose the personal sense, which suits the letter's interest in Satan's activity in the previous chapter, but "from evil" is equally possible grammatically. The word echoes the "evil people" of verse 2.

verse.text: And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing, and will go on doing, what we command.
May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and into the endurance of Christ.

note.term: the love of God and into the endurance of Christ
note.traditional: the love of God and the steadfastness of Christ; older versions: the patient waiting for Christ

verse.note: Both phrases are open in Greek. "The love of God" may be God's love for them or their love for God, and "the endurance of Christ" may be the endurance Christ himself showed, the endurance he gives, or (as in older versions) patient waiting for Christ. The rendering keeps the Greek's openness; most scholars favour God's love for them and Christ's own endurance as the model.

verse.text: Now we command you, brothers and sisters, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to keep away from every brother or sister who lives in an undisciplined way and not according to the tradition they received from us.
verse.note: The word means out of order, not keeping to one's proper place or duty, and was used of soldiers out of rank and of workers absent from their duties. Many modern translations render it "idle" because the context concerns refusing to work, and that is clearly the form the disorder took here. The word itself is broader, so the translation keeps the general sense here and for the related verb in verse 7.

Manuscripts vary between "they received" and "you received". The edition translated here reads "they", referring to the undisciplined members. The difference does not affect the sense much, since the whole community had received the same teaching.

verse.text: For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us: we were not undisciplined among you,
nor did we eat anyone's bread without paying for it; rather, in toil and hardship we worked night and day so as not to be a burden to any of you,
not that we lack the right, but so as to give you in ourselves an example to imitate.
verse.note: The right in view is that of a travelling teacher to be housed and fed by those he teaches. Paul argues for this right at length in 1 Corinthians 9, while explaining there too that he chose not to use it.

verse.text: For even when we were with you, we used to give you this command: “If anyone is not willing to work, neither should that person eat.”
verse.note: The Greek specifies refusal, not inability: the rule is aimed at those who choose not to work, not at those who cannot work or cannot find work. Older English "will not work" meant the same but is now easily misread as a simple future.

verse.text: For we hear that some among you are living in an undisciplined way, not busy at work but busybodies.

note.term: not busy at work but busybodies
note.traditional: not busy at work, but busybodies

verse.note: The Greek plays on two forms of the same verb: "working" and "working around", that is, meddling in what is not one's concern. The English pun on "busy" reproduces the wordplay.

verse.text: Such people we command and urge in the Lord Jesus Christ to work quietly and eat their own bread.
But as for you, brothers and sisters, do not grow weary of doing what is right.
If anyone does not obey our word in this letter, take note of that person and do not associate with them, so that they may be put to shame.
Yet do not regard them as an enemy, but warn them as a brother or sister.
Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times and in every way. The Lord be with you all.
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand, which is the mark in every letter; this is how I write.
verse.note: Letters were normally dictated to a secretary, and the sender could add the closing lines in his own handwriting as authentication. The point has particular force in this letter, which has already warned (2:2) about a letter falsely claiming to come from the writers.

verse.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
